problem: Existing VLN approaches do not fully exploit cross-modal object information, i.e. object references in instructions and object features in the visual scene, and so align them poorly.
motivation: Instructions refer to objects as landmarks along the path, so grounding these references in visual object features should help the agent localize and follow the route. The paper reports the gains are larger on longer, object-heavy instructions.
key_idea: A cross-modal object-aware transformer fuses and aligns linguistic object references with visual object features, so that language provides semantic context for visual object features.
insight: Only the abstract was available, so the mechanism details are not known. The paper's analysis reports the model does better on longer instructions with many object references. It reads this as evidence that the model uses object features and aligns them to instruction references. No ablation details are available.
method: Object-aware transformer: a transformer VLN network that takes object-level cross-modal data as input
Cross-modal object fusion and alignment: fuses and aligns the two cue features of object reference (linguistic and visual) to help the agent capture object features
Linguistic object processing: supplies semantic-level contextual information for the visual object features

setting.backbone: Transformer-based VLN network (details not given in the abstract)
setting.training_data: Not stated in the abstract; presumably R2R and R4R training data
setting.observation: Not stated; presumably panoramic RGB plus object features
setting.action_space: Not stated; presumably discrete nav-graph viewpoints (R2R/R4R)

numbers_note: Abstract only; the abstract gives relative gains (+1.6% absolute SPL on R2R, +2.1% CLS on R4R) but no absolute values or split names.
results: The abstract reports an absolute improvement of 1.6% SPL on R2R and 2.1% CLS on R4R over prior methods (baselines not named). Gains are larger on longer, heavily object-referenced instructions.
limitations: Only the abstract was available, so specifics of the architecture, training and baselines are unknown
Gains are modest and depend on object references being present in the instructions
